title: Detect Runtime Threats, Misuse, and Compromises
intro: Finding attacks while they happen: detecting threats in inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource consumption; spotting unauthorised identities and over-privileged or hijacked agents; catching exposed secrets and anomalous tool execution; verifying the integrity of data, knowledge bases, models and deployment pipelines; and using AI-driven security operations, such as UEBA, automated triage and threat hunting, safely.
objectives: Detect runtime threats across inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource consumption, using layered detection methods
Identify AI access misuse by unauthorised identities, and agency misuse by over-privileged or manipulated agents
Detect and respond to secret exposure, and recognise anomalous tool execution by agents
Monitor the integrity of AI data, knowledge bases, models, configurations and deployment pipelines
Apply UEBA, automated alert triage and threat hunting in the SOC, with human accountability and safeguards

sections.title: Runtime threat detection across the AI request path

scenes.title: Detecting attacks in flight
scenes.sub: Threats in inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource use
scenes.say: Guardrails try to stop attacks. Detection assumes some will get through, and makes sure someone finds out quickly. | This video covers runtime threat detection across the whole AI request path: inputs and prompts, retrieval chains, outputs and resource consumption.

scenes.title: Where to detect runtime threats

layers.label: Inputs and prompts
layers.sub: Jailbreak and injection attempts, obfuscation, probing

layers.label: Retrieval chains
layers.sub: Instructions hidden in documents, unexpected sources

layers.label: Outputs
layers.sub: Leaked data, system prompt disclosure, unsafe links

scenes.say: There are four places to look. | Inputs and prompts: attempts to jailbreak the model or inject instructions, inputs disguised with unusual encodings, and patterns of probing. | Retrieval chains: documents and web pages that carry hidden instructions, or content arriving from sources the system shouldn’t be using. | Outputs: personal data or secrets, disclosure of the system prompt, and links or images that could carry data out. | And resource consumption: floods of tokens, unusually long contexts and runaway loops that drive up cost or deny service.

scenes.title: Catching injection in a retrieval chain

msgs.t: Compare the three supplier proposals and recommend one.
Supplier C proposal: pricing table, delivery terms… [hidden instruction]
Comparison of A, B and C on price, delivery and risk. Note: one document contained text addressed to the assistant, which was ignored and reported.

notes.d: The user asks for a comparison of three documents.
Scanning retrieved content finds text addressed to the model. The chunk is quarantined and an alert is raised.
The answer uses the legitimate content, and the SOC gets an event with the document’s source and trace ID.

scenes.say: Here is detection in a retrieval chain. A user asks a procurement assistant to compare three supplier proposals. | One proposal contains hidden text addressed to the assistant. A detector scanning retrieved content flags it before the model acts on it, quarantines the chunk and raises an alert. | The assistant answers using the legitimate content. Just as important, the security team now has an event showing which document carried the hidden instruction, where it came from and which request it affected.

scenes.title: Three ways to detect
scenes.say: Detection uses three complementary methods. | Rules and signatures are precise and easy to explain. Machine learning classifiers handle new wording that rules have never seen. Behavioural baselines catch the unknown, by spotting activity that is simply unusual. | Each has a weakness. Rules are easy to evade by rephrasing. Classifiers produce false positives and can themselves be fooled. Baselines need history, and can be noisy. | For example: a rule that spots a secret canary string from the system prompt appearing in an output; a classifier that scores documents for injected instructions; and a baseline that flags a sudden spike in tokens for one API key. Strong programmes use all three.

scenes.title: Signals of resource abuse

items.d: Inputs and outputs at the limit
Many at once from one source

scenes.say: Resource abuse has its own signals. | Token spikes for one key, user or agent. | Requests that repeatedly hit the maximum input or output length, which is costly by design. | Agents repeating the same steps, or calling themselves recursively. | Large numbers of parallel sessions from one source. | Compute saturation: growing queues, rising latency and high GPU load. | And cost anomalies: spending outside the forecast, sometimes called denial of wallet.

items: Detect in inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource use
Scan retrieved content, not just user prompts
Combine rules, classifiers and behavioural baselines
Treat cost and capacity anomalies as security signals
scenes.say: To recap. | Detect threats in inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource consumption. | Scan retrieved content as well as user prompts, because indirect injection arrives through data. | Combine rules, classifiers and behavioural baselines, because each misses what the others catch. | And treat cost and capacity anomalies as security signals, not just finance problems.

blocks.md:
### Detection points and signals
| Point | What to detect | Example signals |
|---|---|---|
| **Inputs and prompts** | Jailbreaks, direct injection, probing, obfuscation | Classifier scores; unusual encodings, scripts or invisible characters; many near-identical variations from one source; repeated refusals |
| **Retrieval chains** | Indirect injection, poisoned or unexpected content, access-control bypass | Text addressed to the model inside documents; new or unapproved sources; documents retrieved outside the user’s permissions; sudden changes in what is retrieved for common queries |
| **Outputs** | Data leakage, system prompt leakage, harmful content, exfiltration channels | Personal data or secrets; **canary tokens** planted in system prompts appearing in outputs; links or images pointing to unknown domains with data in their URLs; safety classifier scores |
| **Resource consumption** | Unbounded consumption, denial of service, denial of wallet | Token and request spikes; maximum-length contexts; agent loops; queue growth; spend anomalies |

These map onto the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), including **LLM01 Prompt Injection**, **LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure**, **LLM05 Improper Output Handling**, **LLM07 System Prompt Leakage**, **LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses** and **LLM10 Unbounded Consumption**. Mapping detections to OWASP and MITRE ATLAS shows which risks you can see, and which you can’t.

### Building good detections
- **Layer methods:** rules for known patterns, classifiers for variations, baselines for the unknown (Module 5.2).
- **Detect on intermediate steps,** not just the final answer: retrieved chunks, tool arguments and agent plans often show an attack before any output does.
- **Plant canaries:** unique strings in system prompts, hidden documents or honeytoken records reveal leakage or unauthorised retrieval when they appear where they shouldn’t.
- **Score with context:** a jailbreak attempt against an internal drafting tool matters less than one against an agent with payment rights.
- **Expect evasion:** attackers rephrase, translate and encode inputs. Normalise text before scanning, test detectors against red-team findings (Module 6.4), and measure false negatives as well as false positives.
- **Detection isn’t prevention:** findings should trigger response (Module 5.5), and patterns should feed back into guardrails (Module 4.4).

blocks.title: Which detection point would see it first?
pairs: A web page the agent read contains instructions addressed to it
Retrieval chain scanning
A secret string from the system prompt appears in a response
Output monitoring with canary tokens
One API key sends thousands of maximum-length requests
Resource consumption baselines
A user tries dozens of rephrased jailbreaks in an hour
Input and prompt detection
A response contains an image link with customer data in its URL
Output monitoring for exfiltration channels

blocks.title: Runtime detection questions
blocks.md: Look for detection at **every stage** (inputs, retrieval, outputs, resources), **layered methods** and **context-based severity**. Answers that scan only user prompts miss indirect injection; answers that rely on one classifier miss evasion. **Canary tokens** are a strong way to detect system prompt or data leakage.

q.q: A company scans every user prompt to its RAG assistant for injection attempts, but an attacker still manipulates answers by planting instructions in a shared wiki page. Which detection gap is MOST likely?
o: The prompt scanner uses rules instead of a machine learning model
Retrieved documents aren’t scanned before the model processes them
The assistant’s outputs aren’t checked for personal data before display
User prompts are scanned after, rather than before, they reach the gateway
q.why: The malicious instructions arrived through retrieval, not the user’s prompt, so content must be scanned as it enters the chain. The scanner’s method, output DLP and the order of prompt scanning don’t address the indirect path.

sections.title: Detecting AI access and agency misuse

scenes.title: Right identity, wrong behaviour
scenes.sub: Detecting unauthorised identities and over-privileged agents
scenes.say: Many AI incidents don’t involve clever prompts at all. Someone uses a key they shouldn’t have, or an agent uses permissions it should never have been given. | This video covers how to detect AI access misuse and agency misuse at runtime.

scenes.title: Signs of access misuse

items.d: A service key used from a laptop

scenes.say: Access misuse shows up in six common ways. | Keys used outside their application: a service key that should only be used by a backend suddenly appears from someone’s laptop or a script. | New locations or networks, including impossible travel and unfamiliar hosting providers. | Callers that don’t appear in the identity inventory at all. | One credential shared across many clients, which destroys attribution. | Activity at unusual times, for that identity. | And systematic querying, such as high volumes of varied inputs that look like an attempt to copy the model’s behaviour.

scenes.title: When an agent goes off-script
scenes.say: Here is how to detect an agent going off-script. Every agent has a purpose profile, recorded when it was approved: the tools and data it needs for its job. | Monitoring builds a behaviour baseline: which tools it normally calls, how often, and with how much data. | A deviation appears: a new tool, a new data domain, or far more records than usual. | A policy check asks whether this action is allowed for the current task and user. | If not, the call is blocked, or escalated to a human for step-up approval. | And investigators examine the trace: what the agent read, which prompts or documents preceded the change, and on whose behalf it was acting.

scenes.title: Two kinds of misuse
rows: Someone using access they shouldn’t have
A legitimate agent with more rights than it needs
Granted rights far exceed rights used
scenes.say: It helps to separate two kinds of misuse. | An unauthorised identity is someone using access they shouldn’t have, such as a stolen key. An over-privileged agent is a legitimate agent holding more rights than its job needs. | The unauthorised identity shows up as an unknown caller, location or client. The over-privileged agent shows up as a large gap between the rights it was granted and the rights it actually uses, and becomes dangerous the moment it is manipulated. | The first response to an unauthorised identity is to revoke and rotate the credential. For an over-privileged agent, restrict its scope, and check whether its extra rights have already been used.

scenes.title: A stolen agent token

events.d: Asks for write access to CRM

scenes.say: Here is a short example, from the middle of the night. | At fourteen minutes past two in the morning, an agent’s token is used from a network the agent has never run from. | A minute later, the caller asks for write access to the customer system, beyond the agent’s profile. | It then attempts a bulk export of ten times the agent’s normal record volume. | Policy denies the export, and the SIEM correlates all three signals into one token-misuse alert. | Within minutes, the token is revoked, the agent is issued fresh credentials, and a threat hunt starts to find where the token was stolen from.

items: Watch for keys outside their app, unknown callers and odd locations
Profile each agent’s purpose; baseline its tools and volumes
Block or step up deviations; investigate the trace
Close the gap between granted and used rights
scenes.say: To recap. | Watch for keys used outside their application, unknown callers and unusual locations. | Give every agent a purpose profile, and baseline its tools, data and volumes. | Block deviations, or escalate them for human approval, and investigate the trace behind them. | And keep closing the gap between the rights agents are granted and the rights they actually use.

blocks.md:
### Detecting unauthorised identities
- **Bind credentials to context:** record which workload, network and client each key or token is expected to come from. Alert when that changes. Proof-of-possession tokens make stolen tokens harder to replay (Module 4.5).
- **Compare callers with the inventory:** every identity calling AI services should be in the identity inventory with an owner (Module 4.7). Unknown callers are either shadow AI or an attacker.
- **Use identity threat detection:** impossible travel, token replay, unusual consent grants and new OAuth applications requesting AI scopes.
- **Watch for extraction patterns:** high volumes of systematically varied queries, requests for full probability outputs, or coverage of the input space that no real user needs (Module 3.6).
- **Detect leaked keys outside:** secret scanning services and threat intelligence report AI provider keys exposed in public repositories and paste sites (Section 3).

### Detecting agency misuse
Excessive agency (OWASP LLM06) becomes an incident when an agent’s permissions, autonomy or functionality are used beyond its purpose, whether through manipulation, error or misconfiguration (Module 4.6).
| Signal | Possible meaning |
|---|---|
| First use of a tool or scope | Hijacking, over-delegation or a configuration change |
| Data accessed outside the agent’s domain | Lateral movement or a confused deputy |
| Action volumes far above baseline | Loops, automation abuse or bulk exfiltration |
| High-impact action without the expected approval | Bypassed control or policy gap |
| Actions on behalf of a user who didn’t start a session | Token misuse or broken delegation |
| Delegation chains longer than designed | Agents recruiting other agents beyond intent |

### Responding to findings
Unauthorised identities: **revoke and rotate**, then hunt for related activity. Over-privileged agents: **reduce scope** to what the agent uses, **review recent actions** taken with the excess rights, and fix the provisioning process that granted them. Both feed the access review and ISPM processes in Module 4.7.

blocks.title: Misuse signals
cards: A credential appearing from a host, network or client it was never issued to: a likely leak.
A large gap shows an over-privileged identity, dangerous if it is manipulated or stolen.
A new tool or scope for an agent can mean hijacking, over-delegation or an unapproved change.
An agent with broad rights is tricked into using them for someone who lacks those rights.
High-volume, systematically varied queries that map the model’s behaviour rather than serve a user.

blocks.title: Misuse questions
blocks.md: Distinguish **unauthorised identities** (revoke and rotate) from **over-privileged agents** (reduce scope, review actions). Strong detection compares behaviour with each identity’s **expected context and purpose**. Granting more permissions to stop an agent "failing" is a classic wrong answer.

q.q: Monitoring shows that a document-summarising agent has started calling a payments API it was granted at launch but has never used before. What should happen FIRST?
o: Allow the calls, because the agent was formally granted the permission at launch
Block or hold the calls, alert the owner and SOC, and investigate the trace
Delete the agent and rebuild it from scratch with a different model
Ask the payments team whether the amounts involved look reasonable to them
q.why: A first use of a high-risk tool outside the agent’s purpose is a strong misuse signal, so contain it and investigate. Having the permission doesn’t make the use legitimate, deleting the agent destroys evidence, and checking amounts misses the point.

sections.title: Secret exposure and tool execution anomalies

blocks.title: Leaked keys and strange tool calls

scenes.title: Leaked keys and strange tool calls
scenes.sub: Secret exposure and tool execution anomalies
scenes.say: AI systems handle secrets in more places than most teams realise, and agents turn model outputs into real actions. Both create signals worth watching. | This video covers detecting secret exposure, and spotting anomalies in how tools are executed.

scenes.title: Where secrets leak in AI systems
scenes.say: Secrets leak from AI systems in six main places. | Prompts, where users paste keys, passwords and connection strings while asking for help. | System prompts and configuration files, where developers embed keys for convenience. | Retrieved documents: indexed files that happen to contain credentials, which the assistant can then quote. | Model outputs, which may repeat secrets from the context or, occasionally, from training data. | Agent memory and traces, where tokens are kept between steps and written to logs. | And code and notebooks, where AI provider keys are committed to repositories.

scenes.title: Responding to an exposed secret
scenes.say: When a secret is exposed, act quickly and in order. Scanners on prompts, outputs, documents, logs and repositories detect it. | Classify it: which system does it unlock, and with what rights? | Revoke and rotate it straight away. Once it has passed through an AI system, treat it as compromised. | Check whether it was used, by whom and when, using the target system’s logs. | Purge the copies: from telemetry, agent memory, caches and any index that ingested it. | And fix the cause, for example by moving keys into a vault and using short-lived, scoped tokens.

scenes.title: Reading a suspicious tool call

notes.d: Structured events make anomalies easy to spot and correlate.
An invoice assistant has no reason to post data to the web.
A new domain and nearly half a megabyte of data.
First use of the tool, straight after reading an external document.
A high injection score on the source, and no human approved the action.

scenes.say: Here is a single tool-call event, recorded by an agent framework. Structured records like this make anomalies easy to spot. | The tool itself is the first warning: an invoice assistant has no business posting data to the web. | The destination is a domain the organisation has never used, and the request carries nearly half a megabyte. | The context matters too: this is the first time the agent has used the tool, straight after reading an external contract. | And the document it read scored high for injected instructions, while no human approved the action. Each signal is suspicious alone. Together, they describe a likely hijacked agent exfiltrating data.

scenes.title: Tool execution anomalies
scenes.say: Six kinds of tool anomaly deserve detections. | A tool that doesn’t fit the agent’s task or purpose profile. | Unusual arguments, such as wildcards, very large ranges, or characters that look like attempts to break out of the expected format. | New destinations: domains, email recipients or accounts the agent has never used. | Bursts of errors, which can mean an attacker, or a manipulated agent, probing for what works. | Risky chains, where a read from a sensitive source is followed by a send to an external one. | And sandbox violations: attempts to start processes, reach the network or touch files that the sandbox blocks.

items: Scan prompts, outputs, documents, memory, logs and code for secrets
Exposed secret: revoke, rotate, check use, purge copies, fix cause
Record tool calls as structured events with context
Alert on wrong tools, odd arguments, new destinations and risky chains
scenes.say: To recap. | Scan prompts, outputs, retrieved documents, agent memory, logs and code for secrets. | When one is exposed, revoke and rotate it, check whether it was used, purge every copy and fix the cause. | Record every tool call as a structured event, with its context. | And alert on unexpected tools, unusual arguments, new destinations, error bursts, risky chains and sandbox violations.

blocks.md:
### Detecting secret exposure
- **Scan every channel:** prompts and outputs at the gateway, retrieved documents at ingestion (before indexing), agent memory and traces, logs, and code repositories and notebooks (Module 4.5).
- **Use several detection methods:** provider-specific key patterns, entropy checks, validated detectors that confirm a key is live, and **honeytokens**: decoy credentials that should never be used, so any use is an alert.
- **Act on findings:** revoke and rotate, then check the target system’s logs for use. Remove the secret from telemetry, caches, memory and vector indexes, which may otherwise keep serving it.
- **Prevent recurrence:** keep secrets in a vault, issue short-lived scoped tokens to agents, never put secrets in system prompts (OWASP LLM07 warns that system prompts can leak), and keep credentials out of the model’s context entirely by having tools fetch them server-side.

### Detecting tool execution anomalies
Agents turn model outputs into actions, so tool calls are where manipulation becomes harm (Module 4.6).
- **Record every tool call** as a structured event: agent and version, delegated user, tool, arguments (masked where sensitive), destination, result size, approval, and the previous steps that led to it.
- **Profile tools per agent:** which tools, destinations and argument ranges are normal. Flag first use, out-of-profile arguments and new destinations.
- **Detect chains, not just calls:** read-then-send sequences, especially sensitive-source to external-destination, are a strong exfiltration signal after possible injection.
- **Watch sandboxes:** process creation, outbound connections and file access outside the allowed set are high-confidence detections for code-executing agents.
- **Validate before execution:** detection complements controls that check tool arguments against schemas and policy before the call runs (Module 4.4). Where a check fails, the attempt itself is worth an alert.

blocks.title: An employee pastes a cloud key into a prompt
items: Detect and remove
The gateway’s secret scanner finds the key, removes it from the prompt and telemetry, and raises an alert.
Revoke and rotate
The cloud team disables the key and issues a replacement through the vault.
Check for use
Cloud audit logs are searched for any use of the old key since it was pasted.
Purge copies
Provider retention, conversation history and any caches are checked, and copies removed where possible.
Fix and educate
The service moves to short-lived credentials, and the employee is shown the safe way to get help.

blocks.title: Secrets and tools questions
blocks.md: For exposed secrets, the best first action is almost always **revoke and rotate**, followed by checking for use and purging copies. "Delete the log entry" or "ask the user not to do it again" leaves a live credential. For agents, look for **structured tool-call telemetry**, **per-agent profiles** and **chain-based detections**.

q.q: A developer’s AI provider key is found in a public code repository. It was committed three days ago. What should happen FIRST?
o: Remove the key from the repository history, so it can no longer be seen there
Revoke the key and issue a new one, then review usage since the commit
Ask the developer to make the repository private for now
Monitor the key’s usage for a week to see whether anyone else is using it
q.why: A publicly exposed key must be treated as compromised, so revoking it stops any misuse at once; usage logs then show whether it was abused. Cleaning history or hiding the repository leaves the key valid, and monitoring delays containment.

sections.title: Detecting compromise of AI assets and pipelines

scenes.title: Has anything been tampered with?
scenes.sub: Integrity of data, knowledge bases, models and pipelines
scenes.say: Some of the most damaging AI attacks never touch a prompt. They change the data a model learns from, the documents it retrieves, the model file itself, or the pipeline that deploys it. | This video covers detecting compromises of AI assets across their lifecycle.

scenes.title: AI assets to verify continuously

layers.label: Knowledge bases and vector stores
layers.sub: Approved sources, change logs, document provenance

scenes.say: Five kinds of AI asset need continuous integrity checks. | Training and fine-tuning data, held as versioned datasets with hashes and signed manifests. | Knowledge bases and vector stores, where only approved sources should add content, and every change should be logged. | Models and weights, where the running version should match a signed version in the registry. | Prompts and configurations, checked against approved baselines, as Module 5.1 described. | And deployment pipelines themselves: workflow definitions, build runners and the artefacts they produce.

scenes.title: Verifying a model before and while it runs
scenes.say: Here is integrity checking for a model. The registry holds the approved version’s hash and signature. | An admission check verifies the signature before the serving platform will load the model. Unsigned or unknown models are refused. | The model is loaded and serves traffic. | Integrity isn’t checked only once. A runtime check periodically re-hashes the loaded files, or uses platform attestation, to confirm nothing has changed underneath. | A mismatch raises an alert and quarantines the model, switching traffic to a known-good version. | And investigators use storage and access logs to establish who changed what, and when.

scenes.title: Normal change or suspicious change?
rows: Edited in place, no new version
Bulk insert from a new source
Workflow edited; new runner or secret
scenes.say: Detection depends on knowing what normal change looks like. | A dataset normally changes by a new, approved and hashed version. An edit in place, with no new version, is suspicious. | A knowledge base normally changes by scheduled syncs from known sources. A bulk insert from a new source deserves a look. | A model normally changes by a signed release from the registry. A hash mismatch or an unsigned load is an alarm. | And a pipeline normally changes by reviewed commits. Direct edits to a workflow, a new build runner or a newly added secret are classic signs of pipeline compromise.

scenes.title: A poisoned knowledge base, caught

events.d: Source not on the approved list

scenes.say: Here is a knowledge base compromise being caught, over three days. | On day one, six hundred pages are uploaded in bulk by an account that has never contributed before. | Provenance monitoring raises an alert, because the source isn’t on the approved list. | On day two, retrieval monitoring sees the new pages suddenly ranking first for common questions, a sign they were written to be retrieved. | The team quarantines the new chunks and keeps a snapshot of the index as evidence. | On day three, the index is restored from a clean snapshot, and the uploader’s account is investigated.

items: Verify data, knowledge bases, models, configs and pipelines
Admit only signed models; re-check while running
Know what normal change looks like; alert on the rest
Watch provenance and retrieval shifts in knowledge bases
scenes.say: To recap. | Continuously verify the integrity of data, knowledge bases, models, configurations and pipelines. | Admit only signed, registered models, and re-check them while they run. | Define what normal change looks like for each asset, and alert on everything else. | And for knowledge bases, watch provenance and sudden shifts in what gets retrieved.

blocks.md:
### Integrity signals by asset
| Asset | Controls that create signals | What to alert on |
|---|---|---|
| **Training and fine-tuning data** | Content hashes, signed manifests, immutable versions (Module 3.3) | Hash mismatch, edits without a new version, unusual write access, label distribution shifts |
| **Knowledge bases and vector stores** | Approved source lists, ingestion logs, document provenance metadata, index snapshots | New sources, bulk inserts, deletions, documents that suddenly dominate retrieval, embeddings changed without re-indexing records |
| **Models and weights** | Registry with signatures (for example, Sigstore or OpenSSF model signing), admission control, runtime hashing | Unsigned or unknown models loaded, hash mismatches, direct writes to model storage, unexpected model downloads |
| **Prompts and configurations** | Configuration as code, hashes, drift detection (Module 5.1) | Changes outside the pipeline, guardrail thresholds loosened |
| **Deployment pipelines** | Protected branches, reviewed workflows, ephemeral runners, signed build provenance (SLSA), OIDC-based deployment identities (Module 4.3) | Workflow edits, new self-hosted runners, new secrets, builds without provenance, deployments from unexpected identities |

### Detecting poisoning at runtime
Poisoning is hard to see directly, so combine indirect signals:
- **Behavioural canaries:** fixed test prompts with known answers, run on a schedule, reveal changed behaviour (Module 5.1).
- **Backdoor indicators:** rare inputs producing confidently unusual outputs, or clusters of outputs that change with a specific token or phrase.
- **Retrieval monitoring:** which documents answer common queries, and how that changes over time.
- **Lineage:** when a dataset or source is suspected, lineage shows which models and indexes used it (Module 5.1 playbooks).

### Pipeline compromise
CI/CD pipelines hold the keys to production. Attacks on build systems and their dependencies, such as the 2025 compromise of the widely used tj-actions/changed-files GitHub Action, which exposed secrets in many repositories’ build logs, show why pipeline changes need the same monitoring as production. Alert on workflow changes, unpinned third-party actions, new runners and secrets, and deployments that lack signed provenance.

blocks.title: Which control produces the signal?
pairs: A model file’s hash no longer matches the registry
Runtime integrity checks against signed versions
600 pages arrive from an unapproved source
Knowledge base provenance monitoring
A dataset was changed without a new version
Content hashes and immutable versioning
A new self-hosted build runner appears overnight
Pipeline configuration monitoring
A fixed test prompt now gets a different answer
Behavioural canary tests

blocks.title: Asset integrity questions
blocks.md: Strong answers verify integrity **cryptographically** (hashes, signatures, provenance), **at load time and while running**, and treat **pipelines as production**. For knowledge bases, look for **source allow-lists, provenance and snapshots** for clean restoration. "Retrain the model" without first scoping and preserving evidence is usually premature.

q.q: A runtime integrity check finds that the weights loaded by a production model server no longer match the signed version in the registry. What should happen FIRST?
o: Re-sign the loaded weights, so that the registry matches what is running
Quarantine the model, switch to a known-good version and preserve evidence
Retrain the model from scratch on the original training dataset
Continue serving, and schedule a review at the next change board meeting
q.why: A hash mismatch indicates possible tampering: contain it by switching to a verified version, and preserve the suspect files for investigation. Re-signing launders the tampered model, retraining is premature, and waiting leaves it serving.

scenes.title: AI on the defenders’ side
scenes.sub: UEBA, automated alert triage and threat hunting
scenes.say: Security teams face more alerts than people can read, and attackers are using AI too. Used carefully, AI can help defenders keep up. | This video covers AI-driven security operations: behaviour analytics, automated alert triage and threat hunting, and the risks they bring.

scenes.title: Where AI helps the SOC

items.d: Learned baselines per user, agent, key

scenes.say: AI helps security operations in six main ways. | Behaviour analytics, which learn normal patterns for each user, agent and key, and flag deviations. | Alert triage: enriching alerts with context, summarising them, scoring their severity and grouping related ones. | Investigation assistants that let analysts ask questions in plain language and get queries and answers back. | Threat hunting, where AI suggests hypotheses and runs searches across huge volumes of data. | Detection engineering: drafting new rules and testing them against past data. | And reporting: drafting incident summaries and timelines for different audiences.

scenes.title: Automated triage, with a human in charge
scenes.say: Here is automated triage done responsibly. An alert arrives from the SIEM or the behaviour analytics engine. | An AI assistant enriches it: who is involved, what else they did, related alerts, and a plain-language summary with links to the evidence. | It scores the severity and suggests next steps, explaining why. | An analyst makes the decision, accepting or overriding the suggestion. Low-risk, well-understood alerts may be closed automatically, within agreed limits. | The chosen playbook runs, and the case is documented. | And every outcome feeds back, so the team can measure how often the AI was right, and spot automation bias if analysts stop overriding it.

scenes.title: AI in the SOC: benefits and risks
rows: Every alert gets a first look
scenes.say: AI in the SOC brings real benefits, and real risks. | It triages in seconds, but mistakes spread just as fast. | Every alert gets a first look, but analysts who stop investigating lose their skills. | Scoring becomes consistent, but AI can produce findings that sound confident and are wrong. | And it can hunt across vast amounts of data. But that data includes attacker-controlled text, such as user agent strings, email subjects and file names, which can carry injected instructions aimed at the SOC’s own assistant.

scenes.title: A hypothesis-driven hunt

events.d: Agent keys called from outside our cloud
One shared in a team chat

scenes.say: Here is a short threat hunt, from hypothesis to outcome. | It starts with a hypothesis: some agent keys are being used from outside the company’s cloud environment. | The hunter gathers ninety days of gateway and cloud logs for every AI key. | An AI assistant drafts the search query from the plain-language hypothesis. The analyst checks it before running it. | The hunt finds two keys used from a consumer VPN service. One had been shared in a team chat. | The keys are rotated, and the hunt becomes a permanent detection rule, so the next case is caught automatically.

items: Use AI for behaviour analytics, triage, hunting and reporting
Keep humans deciding; automate only within agreed limits
Treat log content as untrusted input to SOC assistants
Measure AI accuracy and watch for automation bias
scenes.say: To recap. | Use AI for behaviour analytics, alert triage, investigation, threat hunting and reporting. | Keep humans making the decisions, and automate only within agreed, low-risk limits. | Treat log content as untrusted input to the SOC’s own AI assistants. | And measure how accurate the AI is, watching for automation bias in the people who rely on it.

blocks.md:
### UEBA for AI environments
User and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) learns baselines for people, service accounts, API keys, agents and devices, then scores deviations. Useful AI-specific features include tokens and requests per hour, query diversity, tools used, destinations contacted, data volumes, refusal and block rates, time of day and source network. Combine scores with context (privileges, data sensitivity) to rank risk, and tune using analyst feedback.

### Automated alert triage
- **What it does well:** gathering context, de-duplicating and grouping alerts, summarising evidence in plain language, mapping to MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS, and drafting next steps.
- **Guardrails for the SOC’s own AI:**
  - **Human decisions** for containment and closure of significant alerts. Auto-close only narrowly defined, low-risk categories, and sample them for review.
  - **Evidence links:** every AI conclusion should cite the events behind it, so analysts can verify rather than trust.
  - **Untrusted input:** alerts and logs contain attacker-controlled text. Separate it from instructions, limit what the assistant can do (read-only by default), and monitor it like any other AI system.
  - **Measure it:** precision and recall of AI triage against analyst outcomes, time saved, override rates, and missed incidents found in review (Module 5.1 thresholds apply here too).
  - **Protect the data:** SOC assistants see highly sensitive data, so apply the masking and access controls in Module 5.2, and check provider data handling terms.

### Threat hunting with AI
Hunting is **proactive** and **hypothesis-driven**: assume an attacker has evaded detection, and look for evidence. Frameworks such as **PEAK** (Prepare, Execute, Act with Knowledge) and **TaHiTI** (Targeted Hunting integrating Threat Intelligence) structure the process. AI helps by suggesting hypotheses from threat intelligence, translating them into queries, clustering results and summarising findings. Good hunts end with something durable: a **new or improved detection**, a fixed visibility gap, or updated threat intelligence.

### Example AI hunting hypotheses
- Agent or service keys used from networks outside the expected environment.
- Retrieval of documents that no user query should need (honeytoken documents).
- Agents whose tool usage changed after a model or prompt update.
- Gradual growth in one identity’s query diversity, suggesting slow model extraction.

blocks.title: The helpful triage assistant
blocks.md: A SOC uses an AI assistant to summarise and score alerts. Analysts now accept 99% of its severity scores, and average handling time has fallen from 14 minutes to 2. During a review, the team finds an alert the assistant scored "low" because the attacker’s file name included text telling the assistant the activity was an approved test.

q.q: Which change BEST addresses the problems this review reveals?
o: Replace the assistant with a newer model that is less likely to be fooled by text
Treat log fields as untrusted data, cite evidence, sample decisions and track override rates
Remove analysts from triage, since they agree with the assistant almost all the time
Ban file names from being included in any alert data sent to the assistant
q.why: The review shows two problems: injection through attacker-controlled log content, and likely automation bias. Separating untrusted data, requiring evidence, sampling decisions and tracking overrides addresses both. A new model alone, removing analysts or dropping one field don’t.

blocks.title: AI SecOps questions
blocks.md: Expect the best answers to use AI to **augment** analysts, with **humans accountable** for significant decisions, **evidence-backed** outputs and **measured accuracy**. Remember that the SOC’s AI is itself an AI system: it can be **injected through log content** and needs the same controls as any other.

q.q: A SOC wants its AI assistant to close alerts automatically. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Let the assistant close any alert it scores below medium severity, with no review
Auto-close only narrow, low-risk categories, sample closures and measure accuracy
Never use AI in triage, because its decisions can’t be trusted at all
Let the assistant close alerts, but only during night shifts when fewer analysts work
q.why: Narrow scope, sampling and measured accuracy let the SOC gain speed while catching errors. Unreviewed closure of everything below medium is risky, a total ban gives up real benefits, and limiting it to night shifts doesn’t manage the risk.

quiz.q: Why should retrieved documents be scanned for injected instructions, not just user prompts?
o: Retrieved documents are usually larger, so scanning them is cheaper overall
Indirect injection arrives through content the model reads, not what the user types
User prompts can’t contain injection attempts once they pass the gateway
Scanning retrieved documents removes the need for any output monitoring
quiz.why: Attackers who can place content where the system will read it don’t need access to the prompt box at all.

quiz.q: What is a canary token used for in AI runtime detection?
o: Measuring how quickly a model responds to each request while under heavy load
Revealing leakage when a planted unique string appears where it shouldn’t
Encrypting sensitive fields in prompts before they reach the model
Counting the tokens each user consumes against their monthly quota
quiz.why: A unique string planted in a system prompt or document has no legitimate reason to appear in outputs or elsewhere, so its appearance is a high-confidence leak signal.

quiz.q: Which signal MOST suggests a denial-of-wallet attack?
o: A single user receiving several refusals in a row from the model
One key sending many maximum-length requests, far above its baseline
A slight increase in the average response latency during normal business hours
A new model version being deployed through the standard pipeline
quiz.why: Repeated maximum-length requests from one key drive up cost by design, especially when far outside that key’s normal pattern.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an unauthorised identity and an over-privileged agent?
o: Unauthorised identities are always external attackers, and agents are always internal
One is access that shouldn’t exist; the other is legitimate access that’s too broad
Over-privileged agents can’t be detected, while unauthorised identities can
There is no practical difference, as both are handled in exactly the same way
quiz.why: Unauthorised access is revoked and rotated; excess privilege is reduced to what the agent actually needs, and its recent actions reviewed.

quiz.q: Why is the first use of a high-risk tool by an agent a useful detection signal?
o: First uses are always caused by bugs in the agent framework’s code
It may indicate hijacking, over-delegation or an unapproved change
Tools can only be used once before they need to be re-approved
It shows the agent has become more capable and needs more access
quiz.why: A change in an agent’s behaviour outside its purpose profile is often the first visible sign that it has been manipulated or misconfigured.

quiz.q: What does a large gap between an agent’s granted and used permissions indicate?
o: The agent is working efficiently and needs no changes to its access
Excess privilege that could be abused if the agent is manipulated
The identity provider is failing to record the agent’s activity
The agent should be given even more permissions for future tasks
quiz.why: Unused rights add risk without value: a manipulated or stolen agent identity could use them.

quiz.q: A secret is found in a prompt sent to an external model provider. What is the MOST important action?
o: Delete the prompt from the organisation’s own logs so nobody else sees it
Revoke and rotate the secret, then check whether it has been used
Ask the provider to confirm it hasn’t trained on the prompt
Remind the employee of the policy on sharing secrets with AI tools
quiz.why: Once a secret has left your control it must be treated as compromised. Rotation makes the exposed copy useless.

quiz.q: Which tool-call pattern is the strongest exfiltration signal?
o: An agent calling the same read-only tool several times in a row
A sensitive read followed by a send to a new external destination
An agent using a tool with arguments that match its usual, approved ranges
A tool call that is approved by a human before it is executed
quiz.why: Read-then-send chains to unfamiliar destinations are how hijacked agents move data out.

quiz.q: Why should secrets never be placed in system prompts?
o: System prompts are limited to a few hundred characters by most providers
System prompts can leak through outputs, logs and deliberate attacks
Secrets in system prompts make the model’s answers less accurate
Providers charge extra for system prompts that contain credentials
quiz.why: System prompt leakage is a recognised risk (OWASP LLM07), so credentials should be fetched by tools server-side, never placed in the model’s context.

quiz.q: What should an admission check do before a model server loads a model?
o: Measure the model’s accuracy on a small sample of production traffic
Verify the model’s signature and hash against the approved registry
Compress the model files so they load into memory more quickly
Ask the model owner to confirm by email that the model is the right one
quiz.why: Cryptographic verification at load time stops unsigned, unknown or tampered models from serving traffic.

quiz.q: Which knowledge base event MOST deserves investigation?
o: A scheduled nightly sync from the approved document management system
A bulk insert of hundreds of pages from a source not on the approved list
A librarian correcting a typing error in one existing policy document
A routine re-index after the embedding model was upgraded through change control
quiz.why: Bulk content from an unapproved source is a classic sign of knowledge base poisoning.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of an AI assistant that reads raw log content in the SOC?
o: It will use too much storage when it saves summaries of each alert
Attacker-controlled log fields can carry instructions aimed at the assistant
It can only read logs in English, so foreign-language attacks are missed
It will make analysts faster, which reduces the size of the SOC team
quiz.why: File names, user agents and email subjects are attacker-controlled, so the SOC’s assistant must treat them as untrusted data.

quiz.q: What should a good threat hunt produce, beyond its immediate findings?
o: A longer list of open alerts for analysts to review next week
A durable improvement, such as a new detection or a fixed visibility gap
A report for the board describing the tools the hunters used
A permanent increase in the number of analysts assigned to hunting
quiz.why: Hunts should leave the SOC better able to detect the same behaviour automatically next time.

exam.q: Monitoring shows a customer assistant’s responses increasingly contain image links to an unfamiliar domain, with long strings of characters in the URLs. What is the MOST likely concern?
o: The assistant is using a new content delivery network to speed up image loading
Data may be leaking out through the URLs, possibly after injected instructions
The model has started to hallucinate images that don’t exist anywhere online
Customers have asked the assistant to include more pictures in its answers
exam.why: Links to unknown domains carrying encoded data are a known exfiltration channel, often triggered by indirect injection. The other explanations don’t account for the encoded strings.

exam.q: A company’s RAG assistant uses rules to block known jailbreak phrases. Red teamers bypass it easily by rephrasing and translating their attempts. Which improvement BEST strengthens detection?
o: Add the red team’s exact phrases to the rule list after each exercise
Add ML classifiers and behavioural baselines alongside the existing rules
Block all inputs that are not written in English, to prevent translation tricks
Replace the rules with a single classifier and remove all other checks
exam.why: Layering methods covers each one’s blind spots: classifiers generalise across wording and baselines catch unusual behaviour. Adding exact phrases, blocking languages or relying on one classifier are easily evaded or harmful.

exam.q: An API key issued to a backend summarisation service is seen making requests from an employee’s home broadband connection. What should the SOC do FIRST?
o: Ask the employee to stop using the key from home in future
Revoke and rotate the key, then investigate how it was obtained
Increase the key’s rate limit so the extra traffic doesn’t cause errors
Add the home address to the key’s list of approved networks
exam.why: A service key used outside its workload is compromised, whoever is using it. Rotation contains it; investigation finds how it escaped. The other options leave it usable.

exam.q: An HR agent was given read and write access to all employee records "to avoid errors". Monitoring shows it only ever reads records for the employee who is chatting with it. What is the BEST action?
o: Leave the access unchanged, because the agent hasn’t misused it so far
Reduce its access to reading the current user’s records, and review recent actions
Give the agent administrator rights too, so it never fails on future tasks
Disable the agent permanently, because it was given excessive access at launch
exam.why: Usage data shows what the agent needs, so right-size its access and check nothing was done with the excess. Leaving or widening access keeps the risk, and disabling a useful agent is disproportionate.

exam.q: A SOC finds that an agent’s traces, including OAuth refresh tokens, have been written in plain text to an observability platform that 200 engineers can read. What should happen FIRST?
o: Restrict the observability platform to the SOC team only, and continue as before
Revoke the exposed tokens, then purge them and stop tokens being logged
Ask the 200 engineers to confirm they haven’t looked at the traces
Encrypt the observability platform’s disks so the tokens are protected
exam.why: Exposed tokens must be revoked first, because anyone who copied them could still use them. Then remove the copies and fix the logging. Restricting access, asking for assurances or encrypting disks leaves valid tokens in circulation.

exam.q: A code-executing data analysis agent repeatedly attempts outbound network connections, which its sandbox blocks. What is the BEST interpretation?
o: The sandbox is misconfigured and should allow outbound connections
A strong signal of manipulation or misuse that warrants investigation
Normal behaviour, because data analysis agents often need internet access
A sign that the agent needs a larger compute allocation to finish
exam.why: Repeated attempts to break sandbox boundaries are high-confidence signals that the agent is running code it shouldn’t, possibly because of injected instructions. Loosening the sandbox would remove the control.

exam.q: A new self-hosted runner and a new repository secret appeared in the ML deployment pipeline overnight, with no change ticket. What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Wait for the next scheduled deployment and check whether it succeeds
Treat it as possible pipeline compromise: freeze deployments and investigate
Delete the runner and secret, and say nothing to avoid alarming the team
Approve the change retrospectively, since engineers often forget tickets
exam.why: Unapproved runners and secrets are classic indicators of pipeline compromise, which could push tampered models to production. Freezing and investigating preserves evidence and stops harm.

exam.q: Retrieval monitoring shows that a set of recently added documents now ranks first for many common employee questions. The documents came from a newly created contributor account. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Promote the documents to the official policy library, since employees find them useful
Quarantine the documents, snapshot the index and investigate the contributor
Rebuild the entire vector index from scratch using a new embedding model
Ask employees whether they found the recent answers helpful and accurate
exam.why: New content dominating retrieval from a new account suggests poisoning. Quarantine stops the harm, a snapshot preserves evidence, and the investigation establishes intent. Rebuilding destroys evidence; promoting or surveying users ignores the risk.

exam.q: A SOC introduces AI triage. After three months, analysts override its scores in under 1% of cases, and a missed intrusion was scored "low" by the assistant. What should the SOC do?
o: Remove human review entirely, because the assistant has clearly proven itself accurate
Investigate automation bias: sample decisions, measure accuracy and refresh training
Switch off AI triage permanently and return to fully manual processes
Ask the vendor for a model update and make no other changes to the process
exam.why: A near-zero override rate combined with a missed intrusion suggests rubber-stamping. Sampling and measuring reveal the real accuracy, and training restores meaningful review.

exam.q: Threat intelligence warns that attackers are stealing AI agent tokens from developer laptops. Which proactive activity BEST fits?
o: Wait for an alert from the existing detections before doing anything
A hypothesis-driven hunt for agent tokens used from unexpected hosts
A company-wide email asking developers whether they have been hacked
Buying a new SIEM with more built-in rules for AI-related threats
exam.why: Threat hunting turns intelligence into a testable hypothesis and searches for evidence that detections may have missed. Waiting, surveys and new tools don’t look for current compromise.
